function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "# Chapter 9 — Every Cup Twice

*Mission AI: "Water reclamation system operating at ninety-one percent efficiency. Imported water reserves: one thousand eight hundred liters. At current consumption rate of fourteen liters per person per day across thirty crew members, total consumption equals four hundred twenty liters per day. Reserves will sustain the colony for approximately four point three months. I recommend reducing consumption or identifying additional sources."*

*Arun Das: "I know the numbers. Show me the breakdown."*

*Mission AI: "Breakdown follows: potable water thirty-two percent, hygiene twenty-one percent, thermal cooling nineteen percent, greenhouse irrigation fourteen percent, industrial and laboratory use eleven percent, atmospheric humidity recovery three percent."*

*Commander Varga: "Every drop matters. Show the crew."*

---

## Scene 1

Arun stood at the head of the operations module table with a tablet flat in front of him, its screen displaying a single number in large white digits against a dark background.

1800

One thousand eight hundred liters. The entire imported water reserve of the base sat in that number, and Arun had chosen to display it like a countdown clock — which, he would later admit, was exactly what he intended.

The crew gathered around the table in ones and twos, pulling up chairs, leaning against walls, standing where there was no room to sit. It was not a formal briefing. Arun never did formal briefings. He did problem briefings, and the distinction lived in his body language: shoulders squared but not rigid, hands open on the table, eyes moving across the room to make sure everyone was watching the numbers.

Elena stood at his shoulder, arms crossed, face unreadable. She would not interrupt. She would let him run the briefing and step in only if things went sideways.

"Good morning," Arun said. He had a way of saying mundane things that made them sound like the opening of a warning. "I called this together because water is the next thing that can kill us. Not the most dramatic thing. Not a hull breach or a reactor fault. Water is quieter. It runs out while you're doing something else."

He tapped the tablet. The number 1800 stayed on the screen, but a second display appeared below it — a horizontal bar divided into colored segments, each labeled with a system name.

"This is our water. All of it. Every liter in every tank in this base, plus what we can recover from the reclamation system on a good day. Now, I want everyone to look at this and tell me what you see."

Jonah was leaning against the bulkhead with a mug in his hand — a mug containing, Arun noted with quiet irritation, what was almost certainly the crew's most expensive substance by volume. "I see a bar," Jonah said. "With colors."

"Look closer," Arun said. He tapped again, and the bar expanded, the segments separating into discrete blocks with numbers attached.

Thirty-two percent: potable water — the water people actually drank. 576 liters.
Twenty-one percent: hygiene — washing, cleaning, sanitation. 378 liters.
Nineteen percent: thermal cooling — the water that ran through the heat exchangers to keep the reactor and the electronics from cooking themselves. 342 liters.
Fourteen percent: greenhouse irrigation — the water that kept Mei's plants alive. 252 liters.
Eleven percent: industrial and laboratory use — machining, chemical processing, medical prep. 198 liters.
Three percent: atmospheric humidity recovery — the water pulled from the air by the condensers and fed back into the system. 54 liters per day recovered.

"We import water as compressed ice blocks in the cargo holds of the supply ships," Arun said. "We loaded approximately two point two thousand liters at Earth departure. We used about four hundred liters during transit and landing operations — cooling, cleaning, drinking, hygiene, the usual. That leaves the one thousand eight hundred you see on the screen. At four hundred twenty liters per day for thirty people, we have four point three months before the tanks are dry and the reclamation system is the only thing between us and dehydration."

Mei shifted in her chair. A botanist heard the word "greenhouse" and braced instinctively.

"Four point three months," Imani said. She was sitting cross-legged on top of a supply crate, her tablet balanced on her knees, already pulling up her own calculations. "That's a rough number, right? The reclamation system recovers some of that."

Arun nodded. "This is where it gets complicated, and I need everyone to understand the complication. The four hundred twenty liters we consume per day — that doesn't all vanish down a drain, because there are no drains on Mars. We catch it. We filter it. We put it back into the system. Our reclamation system is rated for approximately eighty-five percent recovery under ideal conditions. That means for every liter we use, we get roughly eight hundred fifty milliliters back."

"That still means we lose fifteen percent," Laila said from the back. The physician's voice cut through the room the way her diagnoses always did — clean, direct, inescapable.

"Exactly. Fifteen percent of four hundred twenty is sixty-three liters per day. Lost. Irrecoverable. That's the number that actually matters." Arun brought his hand down on the table — not hard, but with enough force that the water cup at the corner of the table trembled. Everyone's eyes went to it. "Every day, sixty-three liters leave this system forever. They leave through sweat that we can't catch, through breath that goes out the airlocks when people step outside, through chemical reactions that bind water molecules into other compounds, through the tiny fraction that the filters simply can't recover because the physics of separation is not perfect. Sixty-three liters per day. Multiplied by the number of days we have left."

He did the math on the tablet. The number appeared on screen.

241

"The real number, not four point three months. Two hundred forty-one days. Eight months. Maybe nine if the reclamation system performs above spec and we cut consumption hard." He looked around the room. "After that, the tanks are empty. The reclamation system keeps running, but it recycles only what we have. It can't create water from nothing. Without a new source, we slowly run out."

The room was quiet. Not the silence of shock — this was a crew that had already lived through a dust storm and learned that Mars didn't hand them easy numbers. This was the silence of people absorbing a new constraint and beginning the mental work of fitting it into an already-overloaded equation.

"You said the reclamation system is the only thing between us and dehydration," Laila said. "What's 'only' mean in this context?"

"It means if the reclamation system fails for more than forty-eight hours, we start rationing. If it fails for a week, we start making choices about who gets to drink and who doesn't. If it fails for two weeks—"

"Two weeks," Elena said, her voice flat. She didn't need him to finish the sentence.

Arun met her eyes. "Two weeks without water reclamation is a medical event. Dehydration at Mars ambient temperature is not comfortable. The air in this base is kept at low humidity by design — moisture in the air promotes corrosion, mold, condensation damage to electronics. When people stop drinking enough, they start to feel it within hours. Headache, fatigue, reduced cognitive function. Within a day, cramps, nausea. Within three days, organ dysfunction. Within a week"—he paused, not for drama, but because he was choosing his words carefully—"within a week, we lose people."

Jonah set his mug down. The gesture was small, almost unconscious, but everyone noticed. "So we either cut the daily loss below sixty-three liters or we find more water."

"Or both," Arun said. "Preferably both. And that's why I'm showing you this now instead of waiting until the numbers get worse. Because the worst thing a colony can do is not understand its constraints while it still has time to act."

Elena uncrossed her arms. "Show us the plan, Arun."

He turned the tablet to face her. A new screen appeared — a list of systems, ranked by water consumption, with proposed reduction percentages next to each one.

"This is the reduction budget I've been working on. It's aggressive. It will be uncomfortable. And it's the minimum we need to buy ourselves enough time to find local ice."

---

## Scene 2

After the briefing, Arun pulled Mei aside in the corridor between ops and life support. The corridor was narrow — barely wide enough for two people to pass — and it always smelled faintly of ozone and recycled air. Arun had learned to read the base's health by its smells the way a farmer reads the weather. Ozone meant the air scrubbers were working. If the smell changed to something organic, something warm and moist, it meant something was growing where it shouldn't.

Mei didn't need to be pulled aside to know why he wanted to talk. She was a scientist. She had seen the numbers. She had done the same mental math as everyone else and reached the same conclusion: the greenhouse was on the chopping block.

"You're going to ask me to cut irrigation," she said. It wasn't a question.

Arun leaned against the bulkhead and folded his arms. "I'm going to explain the recycling loop first. Then we'll talk about irrigation."

"Fine. Explain."

He pushed off the bulkhead and began walking toward the life support module. Mei followed, keeping pace. The base was never truly quiet — there was always the low hiss of air movement, the hum of pumps, the distant vibration of the reactor cooling loop — but the corridors between modules had a different acoustic quality, a hollowness generated by the thin-pressure atmosphere in the connecting tunnels.

"When you flush a toilet on Earth," Arun said, "the water goes somewhere. It goes to a treatment plant, or a septic tank, or a river, or the ocean. Eventually it evaporates and comes back as rain. The natural water cycle on Earth is enormous — oceans, rivers, groundwater, atmosphere — and the amount humans actually consume is tiny compared to the total. The system absorbs our waste and recycles it naturally. Rain falls. Rivers run. Groundwater recharges."

He stopped at a junction where the main water supply line ran along the ceiling — a thick insulated pipe with pressure gauges mounted at regular intervals.

"On Mars, there is no natural water cycle at this location. No rivers. No rain. The only water is what we brought and what we might find in the ground. We don't have the luxury of a system that absorbs and recycles on its own. We have to build the cycle. Every liter of water that passes through this base — every sip you drink, every gram of moisture in your breath, every drop of sweat on your skin, every gram of runoff from a wash sink — gets captured, processed, purified, and sent back into the system. That is the recycling loop."

He opened a panel on the wall and gestured inside. Behind the access plate was a tangle of pipes, valves, filters, and sensors, arranged in a branching pattern that looked like the root system of a plant.

"This is the primary reclamation manifold. There are three stages. The first stage is mechanical filtration — we catch the large particles, the visible stuff. Hair, skin cells, food particles, whatever else ends up in the greywater. The second stage is chemical treatment — we remove dissolved salts, heavy metals, and organic contaminants using ion exchange resins and activated carbon. The third stage is membrane filtration — reverse osmosis. We push the water through a membrane with pores so small that only water molecules can pass through. Everything else gets left behind."

Mei peered into the panel. "And the rejection?"

"Good question. Reverse osmosis doesn't recover one hundred percent of the water. The process itself loses about five percent of the input volume — it stays behind in the brine stream that we can't process further. That brine gets held in a separate tank, and eventually we either process it through a secondary evaporator or we let it dry out and dispose of the solids. But the point is the loop: waste water enters as greywater, passes through three stages, and exits as potable water. Clean, tested, safe to drink. And then it goes right back into the system to be used again."

He closed the panel and turned to face her.

"The loop is designed for eighty-five percent recovery. But 'recovery' doesn't mean the same volume comes out as goes in. It means that of every hundred liters you put into the system, you get eighty-five liters back out at the other end. The remaining fifteen percent is lost — evaporation, chemical binding, filter absorption, brine rejection, the irrecoverable fraction. That fifteen percent is what kills us if we don't replace it."

Mei was quiet for a moment, her arms crossed, her expression the same one she wore when the greenhouse climate control acted up — focused, analytical, searching for leverage.

"So when you say we need to cut water use, you're really saying we need to cut the fifteen percent loss."

"I'm saying both. We cut the fifteen percent by being smarter about where water goes. Fewer losses mean less replacement demand. But more importantly, we cut the total consumption so that the losses become a smaller absolute number. If we use two hundred liters a day instead of four hundred twenty, the fifteen percent loss is only thirty liters instead of sixty-three. That's the difference between two hundred forty-one days and over five hundred."

"And irrigation?" she said, and now there was an edge in her voice that hadn't been there during the briefing.

Arun didn't flinch from it. "Irrigation water goes into the soil. The plants take up some of it through their roots and transpire it back into the greenhouse atmosphere. We can catch a portion of the transpired moisture with condensers, but not all of it. Some of it gets lost through the greenhouse ventilation system, which we need to run to prevent CO₂ depletion and fungal growth. The greenhouse is currently the second-largest water consumer after personal hygiene, and it has the lowest recovery rate of any system in the base."

"So you want to cut it."

"I want to reduce it to a level where the water input doesn't exceed our ability to recover and replace it."

"Which means cutting it."

Arun held her gaze. The corridor hummed around them, the air moving through the ventilation grates with the steady, indifferent rhythm of a machine that would keep running whether its operators agreed with its priorities or not.

"Mei, I'm not saying the greenhouse doesn't matter. I'm saying that humans have to keep breathing first. People, plants. I can keep people alive with imported oxygen and water reclamation. I can't keep them alive without water, period. The greenhouse is a long-term asset. Water is a short-term emergency. We solve the emergency first."

Mei's jaw tightened. "You're talking about my plants like they're optional."

"I'm talking about thirty human beings who need to drink water every day for the next eight months while we find ice. If we don't find ice, it's not eight months. It's four. And if the reclamation system takes a hit during that time, the math gets worse."

She stood there for a long moment, her arms crossing tighter, her eyes doing that thing they always did when she was running calculations behind her face — rapid, private, unspoken.

"Give me something," she said finally. "Give the greenhouse something. If you cut irrigation to zero, the crops die. If the crops die, we lose the one thing in this base that isn't a powder or a paste. We lose fresh food. We lose the psychological benefit of living plants. And when the imported calorie stores run out — and they will, Arun, you know they will — we'll have nothing."

Arun nodded slowly. He had expected this argument. He respected it, even as he couldn't accommodate it.

"I'll give you forty percent of your current allocation," he said. "That's just under a hundred liters per day. It won't be enough for full production, but it'll keep the mature plants alive."

"Forty percent is not enough."

"It's what I can give you without putting the potable supply at risk. Take it, Mei. Use it wisely. Pick the crops that give you the most calories per liter. Prioritize what you can't replace."

She held his eyes for another few seconds, and he could see the exact moment she made her own internal calculation — the same one he had made, just with different weightings.

"Fine," she said. "Forty percent. But I'm going to make every drop count. And when you find that ice, I want first access for greenhouse expansion."

"When we find the ice," Arun said, "I'll give you a fire hose."

---

## Scene 3

The mess hall — officially the galley module, though everyone called it the mess — was the social heart of the base. It was where the crew ate, where they gathered after shifts, where informal conversations became formal decisions and grievances surfaced over trays of rehydrated food. It was also, Arun realized as he entered it that evening, where the new reality of water rationing would become personal.

The galley module had been designed for comfort — relative comfort, anyway. Earth-like. Tables with fixed seating, warm lighting, a small recreation station with a screen that played downloaded movies nobody had time to watch for more than twenty minutes at a stretch. The walls were painted a soft grey to simulate the neutrality of an interior on Earth, a color chosen by psychologists who had determined that certain visual environments reduced stress in isolated populations.

Right now, the tables were half full. The dinner shift crew — the people whose rotation landed them eating at the traditional evening hour — sat in small groups, eating the current menu: rehydrated chicken stew, compressed grain bars, and a small portion of Mei's greenhouse greens that had become a prized addition to every tray.

Arun took his tray and sat down at a table with Laila and Gabriel. Gabriel had his recorder running on the table — a habit he'd adopted since the all-hands meeting in Chapter 7, when he'd begun documenting everything as if he were writing the first history of a place that might not survive to have a second historian.

"What were the numbers?" Laila asked.

Arun set his spoon down. "One thousand eight hundred liters. Four point three months at current consumption, two hundred forty-one days if you account for the reclamation loss rate. I'm proposing a baseline cut of twenty percent across all non-critical systems."

"Non-critical," Laila repeated. "Define non-critical."

"Everything that isn't drinking, cooling, or oxygen production."

"So hygiene."

"Yes."

Gabriel stopped recording. "What does a twenty percent cut to hygiene look like in practice?"

Arun took a breath. He had spent his career thinking of water as a fluid mechanics problem — flow rates, pressure differentials, pipe diameters, filter efficiencies. He had not spent enough time thinking about what it meant to tell people they couldn't wash themselves properly.

"It means showers get reduced from ten minutes to four. Twice a week instead of daily. Hand washing stays — I'm not going to compromise that, not with Laila breathing down my neck about infection control. But everything else gets tighter. Laundry is suspended indefinitely. We switch to antimicrobial wipes for surface cleaning. Dishwashing uses recycled greywater instead of potable."

Silence settled over the table. Laila's expression was neutral — the physician's mask of professional assessment. Gabriel simply looked down at his tray.

"You're telling me we get to shower twice a week," Laila said. "For four minutes."

"Four minutes of actual water flow. The rest is prep and dry time. Yes."

"Medical showers stay at full allocation, correct?" Laila asked. "Wound cleaning, patient hygiene, surgical prep?"

"Yes," Arun said immediately. "Medical is exempt. Always."

"Good." She took a bite of her stew, chewing thoughtfully. "You should know that on a colony of thirty adults, personal hygiene is not a luxury. Skin conditions, fungal infections, bacterial growth — all of those increase when people can't wash properly. You're trading water savings against medical risk."

"I've factored that in. The forty percent reduction is the maximum I can justify without creating a genuine health hazard. If we go lower, we'll have problems. If we don't go lower, we'll have different problems."

Laila nodded slowly. "I'll accept it. For now. But I want a medical override clause written into the rationing protocol. If I see infections spiking, I reserve the right to increase hygiene allocations without going through engineering approval."

Arun considered this. It would complicate his budgeting — taking water from one allocation and giving it to another meant taking it from somewhere else, and the cascade of adjustments could destabilize the whole system. But he also knew that Laila was right, and that arguing with her on medical grounds was a losing proposition.

"Fine," he said. "Medical override clause. But you have to tell me before you pull the water, not after. I need time to adjust the other allocations."

"Agreed."

Gabriel turned his recorder back on. "Can I ask a question that's not technical?"

Arun braced. "Ask."

"How do you tell people that they can't take a proper shower anymore?"

Arun looked around the mess hall. People were eating, talking, laughing quietly. A few of them were glancing at the water dispenser on the far wall — a small machine that dispensed measured portions of purified water into cups and bottles. It had been a background feature of the base for months, like a water cooler in an office. Nobody had paid it much attention.

Today, Arun noticed, they were all looking at it.

---

## Scene 4

The realization that showers were now an engineering event didn't hit everyone at once. It happened in waves — the way a dust storm hit, not all at once, but spreading from one person to another as the information moved through the base via conversation and observation.

The first wave was practical curiosity. People approached the engineering desk with questions: How long is the new shower timer? Can we schedule our showers around work shifts? Is there a booking system for the water stations? These were the questions of people trying to adapt, trying to fit the new constraint into their daily routines without too much disruption.

The second wave was irritation. The shower timer was a simple countdown clock mounted on the wall of each shower stall — a digital display counting down from four minutes in bright green numbers. When the clock hit zero, a buzzer sounded and the water shut off automatically. There was no override. There was no way to extend the timer without going to engineering and making a formal request.

People who were accustomed to spending ten or fifteen minutes in a shower found themselves racing against the clock. Water that had once been an abundant comfort — something you turned on and stood under without thinking — became a resource to be metered, guarded, and resented.

Remy Okoro, a geologist who had spent the first five weeks of the mission doing field surveys and exterior sample collection, discovered the new limit the hard way. He had come back from an eight-hour exterior run caked in the fine red dust that adhered to his suit and skin like powdered rust. He stripped off his underlayer and stepped into the shower, set the timer, and began washing. The buzzer went off at three minutes and forty-two seconds.

Remy stood naked under the dry showerhead, covered in half-rinsed dust, and said a phrase that Gabriel later described in the Founding Record as "colorful, inventive, and historically significant as an expression of Martian frustration."

Arun found him twenty minutes later, still in the shower stall, trying to argue with the timer.

"It's not personal," Arun said from the corridor, not even entering the stall. "The timer is connected to the water distribution manifold. It's not a suggestion. It's a valve."

"I haven't even rinsed yet," Remy said.

"I know. I'm sorry. But the valve doesn't care. The water budget doesn't care. The budget is a mathematical reality, and mathematical realities are the only kind that matter on Mars."

Remy stepped out of the shower, dripping, furious. "So what — I just walk around with dust on me from now on?"

"Wipe down with antimicrobial cloths before you shower. That's the new protocol. The shower is for final cleaning only. Four minutes is enough for final cleaning if you're efficient."

"Efficient." Remy repeated the word as if it were a foreign language. "I'm not a machine, Arun."

"No. But the water budget is. And right now, the machine is winning."

The third wave was the mess hall incident, and it was the one that Arun had been most concerned about, because it was the moment the water constraint stopped being a technical problem and became a social problem.

It started with a spilled drink — a trivial event on Earth, a nuisance elsewhere. On the base, it became something else entirely.

Sofia Vasquez — no relation to the commander, though she sometimes joked that the shared name should entitle her to special privileges — was carrying a cup of reconstituted fruit drink from the dispenser to her table when she tripped over a cable that had come loose from the floor conduit. The cup tipped. Approximately three hundred milliliters of liquid hit the floor.

The sound it made — a small splash, then a spreading puddle — was not dramatic. But it caught attention. People nearby stopped eating and watched the liquid spread across the floor tiles, a bright orange pool in the dull grey of the mess hall.

Arun was at the far end of the room, eating with Laila and Gabriel, when someone called out: "Hey — Sofia spilled."

Arun stood up. He didn't mean to. It was a reaction, not a decision, and it surprised even him. But he was across the room before he had consciously chosen to move.

Sofia was already on her knees with a roll of absorbent pads, mopping up the spill with frantic, guilty movements. Her face was red — not from exertion, from embarrassment. People were watching. Not staring, exactly, but watching. The kind of watching that happens when a small event becomes a symbol.

"It's fine," Arun said, crouching beside her. "It's three hundred milliliters. It's nothing."

"It's not nothing," Sofia said, her voice tight. "It's three hundred milliliters of purified water that went into the floor drain instead of the reclamation system. It's gone. It's wasted."

"It'll get caught in the floor drain," Arun said, though he knew — because he had designed the system — that the floor drain fed into a secondary greywater tank, and from there it would be pumped to the reclamation manifold and processed like any other grey water. It would be recovered. Not all of it, but most. "It's not gone. It'll be recovered."

Sofia shook her head. "Not all of it. You said fifteen percent is lost. That means forty-five milliliters of this spill just vanished into the air. Forty-five milliliters. And I'm sitting here watching you tell people to shower for four minutes."

The room was very quiet. Arun realized that everyone was listening.

He stood slowly and looked around at the faces — thirty people, his crew, the people he was responsible for keeping alive. They were tired. They had survived a dust storm. They were living on reduced power, eating rehydrated food, working longer hours to compensate for lost productivity. And now they were being told that even the most basic of human comforts was going to be measured and restricted.

He could have given them a technical explanation. He could have talked about the reclamation system, the recovery rates, the budget, the math. He could have been precise and correct and entirely unhelpful.

Instead, he did something out of character for an engineer. He chose words over data.

"Every cup twice," he said. The phrase came from somewhere deep — not training, not planning, but from the same place that had made him look at the 1800 on his screen and see a countdown. "That's what it is. On Mars, every cup of water has to be used twice. Three times. As many times as we can make it last. Because there's no river to go to. There's no rain coming. There's only what we have and what we can recover."

He picked up one of the absorbent pads from the floor and held it up. It was soaked through, heavy with the spilled drink.

"This pad is going to the greywater tank. The water in it will be processed. Most of it will come back clean. Some won't. That's the fifteen percent. That's the part that's gone forever." He looked at Sofia. "And your guilt about it is real, but it doesn't help. What helps is not spilling things. What helps is being careful. What helps is understanding that on this world, water is not a commodity. It's time. Wasting water is the same as wasting time. And we don't have much of either."

Sofia looked down at the empty cup in her hands and nodded. Once.

The quiet in the room lasted a few seconds longer. Then someone — it was Jonah, because Jonah was the kind of person who broke tension with humor even when he didn't mean to — spoke from the back.

"Well. That was the most poetic thing I've ever heard an engineer say about a spilled beverage."

A few people laughed. Not a lot. Enough.

The moment passed. The mess hall returned to its normal murmur of conversation and clinking utensils. But something had shifted. The water constraint was no longer just a number on Arun's screen. It was a thing everyone understood, in their hands, in their routines, in the guilt of a spilled cup.

---

## Scene 5

Imani found Arun in the engineering bay three hours after the mess hall incident, running calibration checks on the water reclamation sensors. The bay was narrow and cluttered — a long room lined with workbenches, tool racks, test equipment, and the kind of organized chaos that Arun considered a sign of a working mind. Schematics were taped to the walls. Spare parts were organized in labeled bins. Three-dimensional models of pipe junctions and valve assemblies occupied the central workbench, arranged in the order they needed to be assembled.

"I've been running route models," Imani said. She stood in the doorway, her tablet in one hand, a coffee mug in the other. The mug, Arun noted, had been filled to exactly the rationed amount — no more, no less. Imani was the kind of person who adapted quickly and practically. She didn't waste energy on resentment.

"What kind of models?"

"Ice search routes. The original plan had us surveying the area within five kilometers of the base. Conservative. Safe. But the orbital survey data shows stronger ice signatures beyond that range — about twelve kilometers northeast, in the lee of a partially buried crater rim."

Arun set down his calibration tool and turned to face her. The engineering bay's lighting was harsh — white LEDs that left no shadows — and Imani's face was all angles and determination under that light.

"Twelve kilometers," he said.

"Twelve point three. One-way. Round trip is twenty-four point six. With a rover carrying drill equipment, sample containers, heater units, and a two-person crew, we're looking at an eight-hour mission minimum. Possibly ten if the terrain is rough."

"That's a full-day excursion. Not a survey hop. That's a commitment."

Imani set her mug down and pulled up the display on her tablet, projecting it onto the nearest wall. A map appeared — a topographical rendering of the landing zone and surrounding terrain, overlaid with orbital survey data. The map showed the base as a small cluster of symbols in the center, with a series of concentric circles radiating outward. The innermost circle — five kilometers — was shaded pale blue. The outer ring — ten to fifteen kilometers — was shaded deep blue.

"The inner ring shows weak to moderate ice signatures," Imani said, pointing. "Hydrated minerals, bound water in the regolith. The kind of stuff Chapter 10 was built on, if that matters. But beyond the five-kilometer ring, the signatures get stronger. This deep blue zone — this is what orbital radar picked up. Subsurface reflections consistent with buried ice deposits. Clean ice, not bound water. Ice you can drill into and melt."

Arun stepped closer to the projection, studying the map. He was not a geologist. He couldn't interpret subsurface radar signatures the way Imani could. But he understood risk, and he understood distance.

"What's the terrain like between here and there?"

"Mostly flat — the plain we landed on extends northeast for about eight kilometers. Then the ground starts rising as it approaches the crater rim. The last four kilometers will be incline, but it's gradual — maybe five to eight degrees. The rover can handle it. I've run the simulation."

"And if the rover breaks down twelve kilometers from the base?"

"Then we walk. We carry emergency oxygen, water, and thermal gear. It's not ideal, but it's survivable. The atmosphere won't kill us in the open for a few hours if our suits hold."

A few hours. The phrase sat in the air between them.

"If we don't find ice," Arun said, "we've spent a day away from the base, burning power, consuming water, consuming supplies, with nothing to show for it."

"If we do find ice," Imani said, "we've changed the math. Not gradually. Fundamentally. Arun, you said we have eight months at the current loss rate. If we find buried ice — real ice, not bound moisture — we can set up an extraction operation. Melt it. Process it. Feed it into the tanks. That doesn't just extend the timeline. It creates a renewable source. We go from counting down to counting up."

She was right. He knew she was right. And that was precisely what frightened him, because being right and being safe were not always the same thing.

"The rover," he said. "It's rated for the terrain we've tested it on. This is untested terrain. There could be buried rocks, subsurface voids, unstable regolith. The dust storm last month could have shifted the surface in ways we can't see from orbit."

"I've accounted for that in the route model. We stay on the flattest possible path. We go slow. We send a robot scout ahead if the terrain looks uncertain. This isn't reckless, Arun. It's calculated."

He turned away from the projection and leaned against the workbench, his arms folded. The models on the bench — pipe junctions and valve assemblies — sat in silence, inert pieces of plastic and metal waiting for the hands that would make them function.

"You know what concerns me," he said. "Not the terrain. Not the rover. Not even the distance. What concerns me is what happens if we find nothing. If we go all the way out there, drill into the ground, come up with bound moisture and dust, and come home empty-handed."

Imani was quiet for a moment. Then she said, "Then we look somewhere else."

"That's what you say now. But people's expectations have built up around this. If we promise them ice and come back with nothing, the psychological damage to the crew will be worse than the physical drain on supplies. Morale is a resource too, Imani. It's not on any of my spreadsheets, but it's real."

"I'm not promising anything. I'm proposing a search. A serious search, at a serious distance, with a serious chance of success. The orbital data supports it. The route is viable. The risk is acceptable."

"Acceptable to whom?"

She met his eyes. "To the person who has to explain to thirty people in three months that we're out of water and there's nowhere left to look."

The silence between them stretched. The engineering bay hummed. Somewhere in the wall, a water pump cycled on — the reclamation system moving greywater through the manifold, turning waste back into resource, one filter at a time.

Arun thought about the water. About the 1800 on his screen. About the four-minute shower timer. About the spilled cup in the mess hall and the way Sofia had looked at it — not as a beverage, but as a piece of time, slipping through the cracks in the floor.

"Fourteen days," he said.

Imani blinked. "What?"

"Give me fourteen days to prep the rover. I want a full mechanical inspection. New seals on every joint. Extra filter capacity for the dust. A secondary power supply. If we're going twelve kilometers into uncharted terrain, that rover better come back. And I want you to run the route simulation three more times with different variables — terrain degradation post-storm, reduced battery capacity, emergency scenario planning. If you can convince me after all of that, I'll approve the mission."

Imani's face was carefully controlled, but he could see the satisfaction in the way she stood a little straighter, in the way she set her tablet down.

"Fourteen days," she said. "I can work with that."

"I'm not promising approval. I'm promising consideration."

"That's more than I had yesterday."

She picked up her mug, took a sip, and set it back down. "Arun."

"Hmm?"

"Thank you."

He looked at her for a moment — this pilot who had flown ships through atmospheres and dust storms and who now wanted to drive a rover into unmapped territory because she believed, with the stubborn faith of a person who had survived too much to stop hoping, that there was ice out there.

"Don't thank me yet," he said. "Thank me when the tank starts filling."

She smiled — a small, tired, genuine smile — and left the bay.

Arun turned back to the calibration work on his bench. The sensor he was adjusting measured the particulate concentration in the reclamation output — the cleanliness of the water after it passed through all three stages. It was sensitive enough to detect particles down to half a micron. On a good day, the output was clear enough to bottle and drink.

He watched the numbers on the display — the concentration reading, the flow rate, the efficiency percentage — and they told him what he already knew: the system was working. It was recovering eighty-nine percent of the water that passed through it today. Better than yesterday. Maybe not as good as tomorrow.

Eighty-nine percent. Eleven percent lost.

He thought about the gap between eighty-nine and one hundred. Eleven percent. In a world where water was time, eleven percent was a lot of time, slipping away, day after day, hour after hour, through the small, inescapable losses that no machine could prevent.

He adjusted the sensor calibration and moved on to the next one.

Outside, through the thick polycarbonate windows of the engineering bay, the Martian landscape stretched flat and empty toward the northeast — toward the crater rim, toward the deep blue zone on the orbital map, toward whatever ice might be buried beneath the ancient, indifferent dust.

*End of Chapter 9 — Bridge: If buried ice exists nearby, everything changes.*
